analysis.one_liner: Bars federal farm and food contractors with serious labor violations from USDA contracts and meat inspections.
analysis.headline: A bill to disqualify federal agriculture contractors with serious labor-law violations, including child-labor abuses, from USDA contracts and meat inspections was introduced with 38 House sponsors and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any company signing a contract with the Department of Agriculture to annually disclose recent labor-law findings against itself or its subcontractors — including child-labor, wage, and safety violations. Companies with serious, repeated, or pervasive violations, or that fail to complete agreed fixes, would go on a Labor Department list and be barred from USDA contracts and from federal meat and poultry inspections for five years, with criminal penalties for knowingly hiding violations. It died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in meatpacking plants, poultry processing, and other agriculture supply chains, especially minors hired by sanitation contractors, who would gain a real enforcement lever: companies that exploit labor would lose federal business and, ultimately, the ability to sell inspected meat.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Meatpacking and farm workers, especially minors

how_it_helps.text: Requires USDA contractors to disclose to the Department of Labor any administrative findings, arbitration awards, or civil judgments for violations of core labor laws — including the Fair Labor Standards Act (which contains child-labor rules), workplace safety law, wage laws, and anti-discrimination laws — covering themselves and their subcontractors [S2] [S3].

Puts companies with serious, repeated, or pervasive violations, or that fail to complete negotiated corrective measures, on a list making them ineligible for USDA contracts for five years, and stops USDA from conducting federal meat and poultry inspections at their facilities — effectively blocking their products from the market [S2] [S3].

Gives companies a path to negotiate corrective measures to avoid the list, so the goal is fixing conditions, not just punishing them, and creates a criminal offense for knowingly failing to disclose violations [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meatpacking companies, poultry processors, and their sanitation and labor subcontractors, which would face disclosure requirements, potential loss of federal contracts, and a five-year ban on federal meat inspection if they commit serious labor violations. Taxpayers would also fund new Labor Department oversight. Some compliance costs could pass through to food prices.

drawbacks.text: Tying federal meat inspection to labor records means a sanctioned plant loses its ability to legally sell meat, which critics would argue could disrupt food supply and raise prices rather than simply change company behavior [S3].

The bill gives the Labor Secretary wide discretion to decide what counts as 'serious, repeated, or pervasive' violations, which business groups would call an unpredictable and potentially overbroad standard for debarment [S3].
Compliance and annual disclosure costs would fall on contractors of every size, including small firms, though the bill allows corrective measures in lieu of the ban [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: in 2023 federal authorities fined a meatpacking sanitation contractor for illegally employing children at plants including major meatpackers' facilities, and the existing enforcement tools clearly failed to prevent it. This bill adds a consequence those companies actually fear — losing USDA business and inspection. The main costs are discretion in the Labor Secretary's hands, compliance burden on contractors, and the blunt instrument of inspection bans; an honest supporter would concede the inspection linkage is aggressive, but the bill's corrective-measure pathway is designed to pull companies back before that point.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Casar introduced the bill on April 25, 2023, and it was immediately referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1] [S5].
Thirty-seven House members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill [S4].

The bill never received a committee markup, hearing, or floor vote; its only recorded action beyond introduction is the referral to committee, and no further action appears through the end of the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meatpacking companies and sanitation subcontractors with labor-law violations are better off: they face no new disclosure requirements and no risk of losing USDA contracts or inspection.

for.name: Rep. Greg Casar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Child Labor Exploitation Accountability Act and organized 37 cosponsors.

for.name: 37 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no further action recorded.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-run Agriculture Committee never acted on the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Major meatpackers sell into a market built on federal inspection; under this bill, companies or their subcontractors with serious labor violations — including child labor — would lose USDA contracts and federal meat and poultry inspection for five years, cutting off their ability to sell product. Their interest in avoiding this runs directly against workers and the minors hired in their supply chains.

industries.industry: Sanitation and labor subcontractors serving packing plants
industries.note: These firms would be covered through the prime contractor's disclosure duty: violations by a subcontractor count against the main contract, and firms committing violations face the same five-year ineligibility. This targets the subcontracting structure that has historically insulated both levels from accountability.

USDA contractors beyond meat processing would face annual disclosure of labor-law findings and criminal penalties for knowingly concealing violations, but only those with serious violations or failed corrections face the ban, and corrective measures offer a way out.
